y-m-27-01.title: If the chance of rain was 70% and it didn't rain
y-m-27-01.topic: The meaning of probability: the chance of rain and the ratio in data gathered many times
y-m-27-01.goal: Tell a single result apart from probability (likelihood), judge how trustworthy a forecast is from the ratio in data gathered over many days, and, each time new data comes out, decide with reasons whether to keep or revise your judgment.
y-m-27-01.material:
The weather forecast said 'tomorrow the chance of rain is 70%', but it did not rain the next day. Seojin said, "The forecast was wrong," and Haeun said, "70% means it rains for 70% of the 24 hours of the day, about 17 hours."
In this task, 'a 70% chance of rain' is taken to mean 'if there are many days with similar forecast conditions, it rains on about 70% of them', and a day on which it rained even a little is counted as a 'day it rained'. Also think about the fact that weather forecasts can have errors. (70% is read as 0.7, or seven times out of ten.)
y-m-27-01.thinking.1: Telling a single result apart from a ratio over many times
y-m-27-01.thinking.2: Revising your judgment with new data
y-m-27-01.prereq.0: Having heard about the meaning of probability (a number expressing how likely something is to happen)
y-m-27-01.prereq.1: Writing fractions and decimals as percentages (grade 6 elementary level)
y-m-27-01.s.s1.prompt: The data is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose your thought, and when the next data comes out, decide whether to keep that thought or revise it.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, calculate '(days it rained) ÷ (days forecast)' and put it side by side with the number in the forecast.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.hint.1: Compare which tells you the accuracy of the forecast: the result of one day or the record of many days.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.0.info: On the day the forecast said the chance of rain was 70%, it did not rain.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.0.ask: From this single result, can you say 'the forecast was wrong'?
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.0.after: A forecast of 70% also carries the meaning 'there is about a 30% chance it won't rain'. So it is hard to assert the forecast was wrong from a single day of no rain. To evaluate a forecast, you need to gather many such days and look at them together.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It did not rain, so this forecast was a wrong forecast
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You drew a conclusion by looking only at the fact that it did not rain. The word 70% also contains a 30% chance that it will not rain.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Even at 70% it may not rain, so it is hard to assert from a single day
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You told a single result apart from likelihood. It would be good to have more data to check this thought.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.0.o.c: 70% means that it keeps raining for about 17 hours that day
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You read probability as a ratio of time. 70% is closer to 'how many of the days is it likely to rain'.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.0.o.d: It did not rain, so the real probability that day was 30%
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You turned the probability around after seeing the result. Even when the result comes out, the likelihood at the time of the forecast does not change.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.1.info: Over the past year, this agency forecast a '70% chance of rain' on 40 days in all, and it rained on 28 of them.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.1.ask: Looking at this data, what would you do with your first thought?
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.1.after: 28÷40=0.7, so this agency's 70% forecasts match the actual ratio of rain. The 12 days it did not rain correspond to the 30% share, so the forecast did not go astray. You can leave the first thought 'it cannot be known from one day's result' as it is, but now you can also state the evidence of the ratio over 40 days.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.1.o.a: All 12 days it did not rain were wrong forecasts, so the forecast is hard to trust
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You counted every day it did not rain as 'wrong'. With a 70% forecast, it is natural for it not to rain about three times out of ten.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.1.o.b: 40 days is plenty, so from now on it will be right exactly as much as 70%
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: 40 days is usable data for making an estimate, but it does not guarantee the future.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.1.o.c: 28/40 is 0.7, which matches 70%, and the 12 days it did not rain do not conflict with the forecast
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You compared the ratio in the data directly with the number in the forecast. The 12 days correspond to the 30% share.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.1.o.d: The first thought, that it cannot be known from one day's result, remains the same even after looking at 40 days
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You kept your first thought. But now there is new evidence, the ratio over 40 days rather than one day, so it would be better to put that evidence into your words.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.2.info: Another forecast app had only 15 days of rain out of 40 days this year on which it forecast a '70% chance of rain'.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.2.ask: What would you think about this app's '70% chance of rain'?
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.2.after: If it is 70%, about 28 of the 40 days are expected to have rain. 15 is 13 days fewer than that, so this app's 70% looks off from the real thing. You cannot say the effect of chance is completely absent, so watching longer is also reasonable. Even so, it is the same that the more evidence there is, the clearer the judgment becomes.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.2.o.a: 15/40 is about 0.38, which is very different from 70%, so this app's 70% is hard to trust
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You revised your judgment by comparing the ratio in the data with the number in the forecast.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.2.o.b: 15 days out of 40 is about the same as 70%
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: If you calculate 15÷40, it is not 0.7. Compare how it differs from the case of 28 days.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.2.o.c: 40 days may be few, so allow for the possibility of chance and watch longer
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This is a careful attitude. However, at 70% about 28 of 40 days are expected, and 15 is 13 days fewer, so the difference is too big to regard as chance.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Even if the apps differ, it is the same 70%, so the results should come out the same
y-m-27-01.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Even with the same number, if the forecasting method differs, how often it is actually right can differ. You have to check with data.
y-m-27-01.s.s1.reflect: Each time the first day's result, the record of 40 days, and the other app's record came out, how did your judgment change (or why did it not change)? How did you connect the number '70%' with the ratio of days it actually rained?
y-m-27-01.s.s2.prompt: Write a reply to Seojin's "The forecast was wrong." Cite the data from the past year (28 of 40 days) as evidence, and also write what more data you would need to know how trustworthy the forecast is.
y-m-27-01.s.s2.hint.0: Decide in what order to compare the two pieces of data: the number in the forecast (70%) and the ratio of days it actually rained.
y-m-27-01.s.s2.hint.1: Start your sentence by separating 'once' and 'many times'.
y-m-27-01.s.s2.placeholder: Example: From the result of a single time alone, ...
y-m-27-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you explain in your own words whether the one day of no rain conflicts with the word 70% or not?
y-m-27-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you use numbers like 28 days and 40 days as evidence?
y-m-27-01.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Could the data you said you need actually be used to evaluate the forecast?
y-m-27-01.s.s2.model.0: You cannot say it was wrong from one day's result alone. A 70% forecast means it might not rain, and over the past year it rained on 28 of the 40 days with a 70% forecast, which matches 70%. To evaluate a forecast, you have to gather many such days and look at the ratio of days it rained.
y-m-27-01.s.s2.model.1: You cannot know from the single time it didn't rain. 28 out of 40 days is 0.7, which is close to 70%. So it is hard to say this forecast was wrong, and with records from more days you could know more surely.

y-m-27-02.title: What is the probability that the thumbtack's point faces up?
y-m-27-02.topic: The meaning of probability: estimating the probability of outcomes that do not occur equally often by relative frequency
y-m-27-02.goal: Understand that just because there are only two outcomes, each probability is not 1/2, estimate the probability from several sets of data with different numbers of throws, and explain how to revise the estimated value when new data comes out.
y-m-27-02.material:
A thumbtack was dropped on a desk, and the way it came to rest was recorded as one of 'point facing up' and 'point lying sideways'. With one throw, these are the only two outcomes; the same thumbtack was dropped on the same floor, and each throw is considered not to affect the others.
Records of four groups (group: number of throws / number of times the point faced up)
Group 1: 10 throws / 7 times
Group 2: 40 throws / 18 times
Group 3: 150 throws / 66 times
Group 4: 800 throws / 349 times
(All four groups together make 440 out of 1000 throws.)
y-m-27-02.thinking.0: Telling the number of outcomes apart from probability
y-m-27-02.thinking.1: Comparing evidence while taking the amount of data into account
y-m-27-02.thinking.2: Revising an estimated value with new data
y-m-27-02.prereq.0: The meaning of probability and expressing it as a number from 0 to 1
y-m-27-02.prereq.1: Writing (number of times an outcome occurred) ÷ (total number of times) as a decimal
y-m-27-02.s.s1.prompt: What is the most fitting way to state the probability that the thumbtack's point faces up?
y-m-27-02.s.s1.hint.0: Write (number of times facing up) ÷ (number of throws) for each of the four groups as a decimal.
y-m-27-02.s.s1.hint.1: Find what you see when you compare the ratios of the groups with few throws and the groups with many throws.
y-m-27-02.s.s1.o.a: There are only two outcomes, so the probability of facing up is exactly 1/2
y-m-27-02.s.s1.r.a: There being two outcomes and the two outcomes occurring equally often are different. Looking at the records, is there a group whose ratio of facing up is over half, or one that is not?
y-m-27-02.s.s1.o.b: The ratio 0.7 (7/10) of Group 1, which threw first, is the value to be the standard
y-m-27-02.s.s1.r.b: This is the ratio of a group with only 10 throws. When there are few throws, the effect of chance can be large. Compare it with the ratios of the other groups.
y-m-27-02.s.s1.o.c: It is 440 out of 1000, so estimate it at about 0.44, but the value may change
y-m-27-02.s.s1.r.c: You based it on data with many throws and also thought that the value may change.
y-m-27-02.s.s1.o.d: The about 0.44 (349/800) of Group 4, which threw the most, is the most trustworthy
y-m-27-02.s.s1.r.d: You based it on the one group with the most throws. It is reasonable since it is almost the same value as the combined one. It would also be good to think about whether there is a reason to discard the other groups.
y-m-27-02.s.s1.o.e: A thumbtack has an uneven shape, so it is difficult even to speak of a probability
y-m-27-02.s.s1.r.e: When you throw many times under constant conditions, you can see the ratio gathering near some value. Compare the ratios of the groups.
y-m-27-02.s.s1.explain: It is 440 out of 1000, so estimating about 0.44 is the judgment that used the data most broadly. The 0.436 (349÷800) of Group 4 alone is almost the same value. As in Group 1's 0.7, Group 2's 0.45, Group 3's 0.44, and Group 4's 0.436, you can see the ratio gathering around 0.44 as the number of throws increases. This value is not a fixed true value but an estimate, so it may change a little if you throw more.
y-m-27-02.s.s1.acc.0: Basing it on the ratio of Group 4, which threw the most (about 0.436), is also reasonable. It is almost the same as the combined value 0.44.
y-m-27-02.s.s2.prompt: A fifth group threw the same thumbtack on the same floor 20 times, and the point faced up 6 times (0.3). Jihu said, "0.3 just came out, so 0.44 is a wrong value." Write what you think about Jihu's statement, with evidence.
y-m-27-02.s.s2.hint.0: Write the number of throws of Group 5 and the combined number of throws of the first four groups side by side and compare them.
y-m-27-02.s.s2.hint.1: Calculate yourself the ratio including the records of Group 5 and compare it with the earlier value.
y-m-27-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you compare the 20 throws with the earlier 1000 and speak about it?
y-m-27-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you think of a way that throws away neither the new data nor the earlier value?
y-m-27-02.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Can you redo the calculation with the numbers you wrote?
y-m-27-02.s.s2.model.0: No. Group 5 threw only 20 times, so 0.3 may have come out by chance. Even if I add these 6 to 440 out of 1000 and find it again as 446 out of 1020, it is about 0.44, so it stays the same.
y-m-27-02.s.s2.model.1: I must not throw away 0.44 right away. 20 throws is few and can swing. I'll first check whether Group 5 threw with the same thumbtack and on the same floor, and if so I'll recalculate by correcting it to 446 out of the combined 1020.

y-m-27-03.title: Making two-digit even numbers with five cards
y-m-27-03.topic: Number of cases: making numbers with conditions (0 cannot be in the tens place, the same card cannot be used twice)
y-m-27-03.goal: Make numbers that fit the conditions (0 cannot be in the tens place, each card is used only once) yourself, and find and explain where counting methods under those conditions easily go wrong.
y-m-27-03.material: There are 5 cards with 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 written on them, one each. Pick 2 different cards from them and place them in order to make a two-digit integer (the card placed first is the tens place and the card placed after is the ones place). 0 cannot be in the tens place (example: 03 is not a two-digit integer). The same card can be used only once (example: 22 cannot be made).
y-m-27-03.thinking.0: Making examples that fit the conditions
y-m-27-03.thinking.2: Finding errors in a counting method
y-m-27-03.prereq.0: The tens place and ones place of a two-digit integer
y-m-27-03.prereq.1: Experience counting the number of ways when several steps of choices follow one another
y-m-27-03.s.s1.prompt: How many two-digit integers in all can be made with these cards?
y-m-27-03.s.s1.hint.0: First write down all the cards that can be in the tens place.
y-m-27-03.s.s1.hint.1: After you choose one card for the tens place, count how many cards remain that can be used for the ones place.
y-m-27-03.s.s1.r.a: This is a calculation counting the first card as 5 ways out of 5 cards. Think about whether you also counted the cases where 0 is placed in the tens place.
y-m-27-03.s.s1.r.b: This is a calculation that looked at how many ways there are for the tens place and the ones place each, and whether they affect each other.
y-m-27-03.s.s1.r.c: You also counted the cases of using the same card twice. Check whether you can make 22 or 44.
y-m-27-03.s.s1.r.d: It seems you counted too few choices for the ones place. After choosing the tens place, count how many cards remain.
y-m-27-03.s.s1.explain: For the tens place, 4 cards, 1, 2, 3, 4, can come, leaving out 0. For the ones place, the other 4 cards (including 0), leaving out the card used in the tens place, can come, so 4×4=16.
y-m-27-03.s.s2.prompt: Make 4 different two-digit even integers while keeping the conditions above. (The number n you made)
y-m-27-03.s.s2.hint.0: First decide what card must be in the ones place for the number to be even.
y-m-27-03.s.s2.hint.1: After choosing the ones-place card, check by crossing out one by one which cards can be used for the tens place.
y-m-27-03.s.s2.var.n: The two-digit even number you made
y-m-27-03.s.s2.fail.c1: The cards are only 0 to 4, so it must be an integer from 10 to 44.
y-m-27-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The tens-place card cannot be 0 and must be chosen only from 0 to 4.
y-m-27-03.s.s2.ok.c3: The ones place is a digit on a card.
y-m-27-03.s.s2.fail.c3: The ones place must also be one of 0 to 4.
y-m-27-03.s.s2.fail.c4: You cannot use the same card twice in the tens place and the ones place.
y-m-27-03.s.s2.fail.c5: It is not even. For an even number, what digit must the ones place be?
y-m-27-03.s.s2.explain: If the ones place is 0, the tens place is 1, 2, 3, 4 (4 numbers); if the ones place is 2, the tens place is 1, 3, 4 (3 numbers); if the ones place is 4, the tens place is 1, 2, 3 (3 numbers); so the even numbers are 10 in all: 10, 12, 14, 20, 24, 30, 32, 34, 40, 42.
y-m-27-03.s.s3.prompt: Seojin calculated, "The even numbers are 4 ways for the tens place × 3 ways for the ones place (0, 2, 4) = 12." What is the most fitting reason this calculation is not right?
y-m-27-03.s.s3.hint.0: List all 12 and compare them with the 10 you checked in s2.
y-m-27-03.s.s3.hint.1: When the ones-place card is 2, list the cards that can be used for the tens place.
y-m-27-03.s.s3.o.a: It is a situation where you should add, not multiply
y-m-27-03.s.s3.r.a: It is a situation where you decide the tens place and then the ones place in turn, so the multiplying method is right. Look at what numbers are mixed in the multiplied value.
y-m-27-03.s.s3.o.b: It did not count the cases where 0 is placed in the tens place
y-m-27-03.s.s3.r.b: The 4 ways for the tens place already counted only 1 to 4. Write out the numbers contained in the 12 yourself and look at them.
y-m-27-03.s.s3.o.c: You have to find more even numbers that can be in the ones place besides 0, 2, 4
y-m-27-03.s.s3.r.c: Among the cards 0 to 4, the even ones are only 0, 2, 4.
y-m-27-03.s.s3.o.d: Numbers that use the same card twice, like 22 and 44, are mixed in the 12
y-m-27-03.s.s3.r.d: If you write out the 12 counted by multiplication yourself, you will see numbers that cannot be made.
y-m-27-03.s.s3.explain: If you multiply 4 ways for the tens place by 3 ways for the ones place, numbers that use the same card twice, like 22 and 44, are mixed into the 12. If you take away these two, 10 is right. Since the number of cards that can be used for the tens place differs as 4, 3, 3 depending on the ones place, there is also a method of counting by dividing up by the ones-place card.

y-m-27-04.title: Does the calculation '20 ways' fit every kind of selection?
y-m-27-04.topic: Number of cases: selections that distinguish order and selections that do not
y-m-27-04.goal: Find why the same calculation gives different results when the chosen people have different roles and when they do not, and correct the number of ways by working out how many times one combination was counted.
y-m-27-04.material:
From 5 members of the choir (가온, 나리, 다솜, 라온, 마루), two tasks are to be decided.
(A) Choose 1 president and 1 vice president. One person cannot hold both positions.
(B) Choose 2 stage-cleaning duty members. There is no difference in the work the two chosen people do.
Eunu solved both tasks as "5×4=20 ways". Eunu's solution goes like this.
y-m-27-04.thinking.0: Finding the hidden assumption in a solution
y-m-27-04.thinking.2: Working out and correcting the number of times something was counted twice
y-m-27-04.prereq.0: Experience counting the number of ways when several steps of choices follow one another
y-m-27-04.prereq.1: Experience listing all the cases by replacing people's names with symbols
y-m-27-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose the one line in Eunu's solution that is hard to believe.
y-m-27-04.s.s1.hint.0: For (A) and (B), work out whether swapping the two chosen people makes a difference or is the same.
y-m-27-04.s.s1.hint.1: Shorten the names to 가, 나, 다, 라, 마 and compare whether (가, 나) and (나, 가) are the same case in (A) and in (B).
y-m-27-04.s.s1.line.0: In (A), the people who can be president are 5.
y-m-27-04.s.s1.line.1: Once the president is decided, the people who can be vice president are the other 4. Therefore (A) is 5×4=20 ways.
y-m-27-04.s.s1.line.2: For (B) too, there are 5 ways to choose the first person first, and then 4 ways to choose the second person.
y-m-27-04.s.s1.line.3: Therefore (B) is also 5×4=20 ways, and the numbers of ways for (A) and (B) are the same.
y-m-27-04.s.s1.explain: Lines 1 and 2 are right. President and vice president are different roles, so (가온 president, 나리 vice president) and (나리 president, 가온 vice president) are different cases, and 20 ways is right. The problem starts at line 3. In (B) there is no difference in roles, so (가온, 나리) and (나리, 가온) are the same duty combination, but if you count by 5×4 you count these two separately and count one combination twice. So the conclusion in line 4 that '(A) and (B) are the same' is wrong too.
y-m-27-04.s.s2.prompt: In how many ways in all can you choose the 2 stage-cleaning duty members for (B)?
y-m-27-04.s.s2.hint.0: Shorten the names to symbols and list the combinations in order, starting with the ones that contain 가.
y-m-27-04.s.s2.hint.1: Count how many times one combination (for example, 가온 and 나리) is contained in the 20 ways.
y-m-27-04.s.s2.r.a: This is the value counted by 5×4. Check whether you counted the cases where the two chosen people are swapped separately.
y-m-27-04.s.s2.r.b: This looks like the value counting only the cases of choosing one person. List the cases of two people being chosen yourself.
y-m-27-04.s.s2.r.c: This is a calculation that counts the same two people with only the order swapped as one.
y-m-27-04.s.s2.r.d: This is the value that even counted choosing the same person twice. The 2 duty members must be different people.
y-m-27-04.s.s2.explain: 5×4=20 is the value that counted the same two people with only the order swapped, like (가온, 나리) and (나리, 가온), separately. Each duty combination was counted twice, so it is 20÷2=10 ways. If you list them directly as 가나, 가다, 가라, 가마, 나다, 나라, 나마, 다라, 다마, 라마, it is also 10 ways.
y-m-27-04.s.s3.prompt: If (B) is changed to "3 duty members", in how many ways in all can you choose 3 of the 5 people? (There is no difference in roles.)
y-m-27-04.s.s3.hint.0: Write down all the orders in which the three people 가, 나, 다 can line up and count how many ways there are.
y-m-27-04.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether you get the same value if you divide up the cases by who is not chosen.
y-m-27-04.s.s3.r.a: This is the value worked out by how many times the same three people are counted. You get the same value if you think in terms of the people who are not chosen.
y-m-27-04.s.s3.r.b: This is the value that stopped after counting 5×4×3. Check whether you counted the same three people several times with only the order swapped.
y-m-27-04.s.s3.r.c: This is the value divided only by 2 as in the case of 2 people. Work out the number of orders in which three people can line up.
y-m-27-04.s.s3.r.d: This is the value that used 5×4 as it is. The process of choosing the third person is missing.
y-m-27-04.s.s3.explain: 5×4×3=60 is the value that also distinguishes the order of choosing the three people. The orders in which the same three people can line up are 3×2×1=6 ways, so each combination is counted 6 times. 60÷6=10 ways. Choosing 3 of 5 people is the same as deciding the 2 people not chosen, so it is also the same as the 10 ways of choosing 2 people.

y-m-27-05.title: If you roll 6 times, will a 6 definitely come up?
y-m-27-05.topic: Calculating probability: can the probability of 'at least once' be found by adding?
y-m-27-05.goal: Make counterexamples yourself to show in what cases the rule 'add the probability for one time as many times as the number of throws' does not hold, and correct the probability for two throws by listing all the cases.
y-m-27-05.material: When throwing one fair die several times, Hayun made a rule about the probability that a 6 comes up at least once. "The probability of getting a 6 in one throw is 1/6. So the probability of getting a 6 at least once in n throws is 1/6 added n times, which is n/6." (The die is fair, and each throw does not affect the others.)
y-m-27-05.thinking.0: Making an example (counterexample) where the rule does not hold
y-m-27-05.thinking.1: Listing all the cases to check
y-m-27-05.thinking.2: Using the range that a probability must stay within
y-m-27-05.prereq.0: The meaning of probability and expressing it as a number from 0 to 1
y-m-27-05.prereq.1: Experience listing the 36 results of throwing two dice as (first number, second number)
y-m-27-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose the one line in Hayun's story that is hard to believe. (It can be the line with the wrong process, or the line where the wrong conclusion because of it is written.)
y-m-27-05.s.s1.hint.0: When writing the result of two throws as (first number, second number), look at which cases contain (6, 6).
y-m-27-05.s.s1.hint.1: With Hayun's rule, calculate the value while increasing the number of throws, like 6, 7, 8.
y-m-27-05.s.s1.line.0: The probability of getting a 6 when throwing a die once is 1/6.
y-m-27-05.s.s1.line.1: The probability of getting a 6 at least once when throwing twice is 1/6+1/6=1/3.
y-m-27-05.s.s1.line.2: In the same way, with 6 throws it is 6/6=1, so a 6 definitely comes up at least once.
y-m-27-05.s.s1.line.3: Therefore it cannot happen that a 6 never comes up in 6 throws.
y-m-27-05.s.s1.explain: Line 1 is right. The problem starts at line 2. The case where (6, 6) comes up in two throws is contained both in 'the case where the first is 6' and 'the case where the second is 6', so if you add 1/6+1/6 this case is counted twice. Because of that, 'with 6 throws the probability is 1' in line 3 and 'it cannot happen that none comes up' in line 4 are wrong too. In fact, with 6 throws a 6 may not come up at all.
y-m-27-05.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter 3 different numbers of throws n for which the probability becomes strange under Hayun's rule. (n is a natural number from 7 to 20)
y-m-27-05.s.s2.hint.0: Think about what range n/6, calculated by the rule, must go outside of so that it cannot be used as a probability.
y-m-27-05.s.s2.hint.1: Put in n a little at a time, like 7, 8, 9, and calculate n/6.
y-m-27-05.s.s2.ok.c1: It is a natural number from 7 to 20.
y-m-27-05.s.s2.fail.c1: Please enter n as a natural number from 7 to 20.
y-m-27-05.s.s2.ok.c2: The n/6 found by the rule is greater than 1, so it is a value that cannot be a probability.
y-m-27-05.s.s2.fail.c2: For this n, n/6 does not go over 1. For n/6 to become a strange value for a probability, n must be greater than what?
y-m-27-05.s.s2.explain: A probability cannot be greater than 1. With 7 throws the rule gives 7/6, with 10 throws 10/6, values that go over 1. Since there are examples where a value that cannot be used as a probability comes out, Hayun's rule does not always hold. When n=6, 1 comes out, but this too differs from the actual probability.
y-m-27-05.s.s3.prompt: What is the probability that a 6 comes up at least once in two throws? Check by counting the 36 results yourself.
y-m-27-05.s.s3.hint.0: Write the results of the two dice as (first, second) and draw the 36 ways in a table.
y-m-27-05.s.s3.hint.1: In that table, count the number of cells that contain at least one 6.
y-m-27-05.s.s3.r.a: This is the value Hayun found. Check by counting among the 36 ways whether (6, 6) was counted twice.
y-m-27-05.s.s3.r.b: This is the value from counting the 36 results yourself and counting the overlapping case only once.
y-m-27-05.s.s3.r.c: This is the probability of the case where a 6 never comes up. You need to find the case where it comes up at least once.
y-m-27-05.s.s3.r.d: This is the value counting only (6, 6). There are also cases where only the first is 6 or only the second is 6.
y-m-27-05.s.s3.explain: Among the 36 ways, the results with at least one 6 are the 6 of (6,1) to (6,6) and the 5 of (1,6) to (5,6), 11 ways in all. The probability is 11/36, which is less than 1/3=12/36. The results with no 6 are 5×5=25 ways, so 36-25=11 gives the same.

y-m-27-06.title: A marble problem whose answers split into two
y-m-27-06.topic: Calculating probability: the difference depending on whether the drawn item is put back when drawing in succession
y-m-27-06.goal: Find out that the missing condition in the problem (whether the drawn marble is put back) decides the answer, compare the probability under each condition, and work out how the difference between the two conditions changes when the number of marbles becomes large.
y-m-27-06.material:
A bag holds 3 red marbles and 2 blue marbles. The marbles differ only in color and have the same shape and size, so with your eyes closed you cannot decide which marble will come out. You take marbles out of this bag one at a time, twice, and check the colors.
Problem: "What is the probability that the two marbles taken out are the same color?"
Eunseo answered 13/25 and Doyun answered 2/5. Neither of them made a mistake in the calculation by their own method. But the problem does not say 'whether the marble taken out is put back in the bag'.
y-m-27-06.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is sufficient
y-m-27-06.thinking.1: Comparing probabilities by dividing into conditions
y-m-27-06.thinking.2: Estimating the change when the numbers become large
y-m-27-06.prereq.0: Experience finding the probability of things that happen several times in succession
y-m-27-06.s.s1.hint.0: Write down how many marbles Eunseo and Doyun each assumed were in the bag at the second draw.
y-m-27-06.s.s1.hint.1: Find where the denominators the two used (5 and 4) become different.
y-m-27-06.s.s1.o.a: Only Eunseo's answer is right. Putting the marble back is the original rule
y-m-27-06.s.s1.r.a: The problem has no words about putting it back. Think about whether you added an assumption yourself, calling it the original rule.
y-m-27-06.s.s1.o.b: Only Doyun's answer is right. Obviously the marble taken out is kept outside
y-m-27-06.s.s1.r.b: The problem also has no words about not putting it back. Think about whether you assumed it as obvious.
y-m-27-06.s.s1.o.c: Both are wrong. There are two colors, so the probability of the same color is 1/2
y-m-27-06.s.s1.r.c: There are more red marbles, so the two colors do not come out equally often. Look at the number of marbles, not the number of colors.
y-m-27-06.s.s1.o.d: It cannot be decided without knowing whether the marble taken out is put back
y-m-27-06.s.s1.r.d: You realized that the missing condition decides the answer. It would be good to check how the value comes out under each condition.
y-m-27-06.s.s1.explain: If you put it back, at the second draw there are still 3 red and 2 blue marbles, so (3/5)×(3/5)+(2/5)×(2/5)=13/25, and if you do not put it back, 4 are left at the second draw, so (3/5)×(2/4)+(2/5)×(1/4)=2/5. The two values are different, so without knowing 'whether it is put back' you cannot decide.
y-m-27-06.s.s2.prompt: What conditions would each of the two answers need in order to be right?
y-m-27-06.s.s2.hint.0: Compare the denominators of the second probability in the two expressions.
y-m-27-06.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether the numerators of the second probability (the number of red marbles, the number of blue marbles) depend on the first result.
y-m-27-06.s.s2.o.a: Eunseo puts it back, Doyun does not put it back
y-m-27-06.s.s2.r.a: Each judged by whether the number of marbles remaining when taking out the second marble is 5 or 4.
y-m-27-06.s.s2.o.b: Eunseo does not put it back, Doyun puts it back
y-m-27-06.s.s2.r.b: Check how many marbles remain at the second draw using Eunseo's expression (denominator 5).
y-m-27-06.s.s2.o.c: Both put it back and only the calculation method differs
y-m-27-06.s.s2.r.c: If you put it back, the denominator is the same 5 when taking out the second marble too. Check Doyun's denominator.
y-m-27-06.s.s2.o.d: Neither puts it back and only the calculation method differs
y-m-27-06.s.s2.r.d: If you do not put it back, the denominator is 4 when taking out the second marble. Check Eunseo's expression.
y-m-27-06.s.s2.explain: Eunseo's expression (3/5)×(3/5)+(2/5)×(2/5) takes the second marble out of 5 again, so it is the case of putting it back. Doyun's expression (3/5)×(2/4)+(2/5)×(1/4) takes the second marble out of 4, so it is the case of not putting it back.
y-m-27-06.s.s3.prompt: If you increase the marbles to 30 red and 20 blue (the ratio is the same, 3:2) and compare the two conditions, what happens to the difference between the two probabilities compared with the start (3 red, 2 blue)?
y-m-27-06.s.s3.hint.0: Write the denominator of the probability of taking out the second marble when not putting it back, for the original situation and for the new situation.
y-m-27-06.s.s3.hint.1: Calculate the probabilities of the two conditions as decimals and compare them side by side with the original difference.
y-m-27-06.s.s3.o.a: The gap becomes larger than at the start
y-m-27-06.s.s3.r.a: Compare how much the marbles remaining after taking one out decrease when the number of marbles is large.
y-m-27-06.s.s3.o.b: It is exactly the same as the original difference
y-m-27-06.s.s3.r.b: Even if the ratio is the same, the number of marbles remaining after taking one out is different. Compare when the denominators are 5 and 4 with when they are 50 and 49.
y-m-27-06.s.s3.o.c: It becomes so small that it almost disappears
y-m-27-06.s.s3.r.c: You caught the point that when there are many marbles, taking out one hardly changes what remains.
y-m-27-06.s.s3.o.d: The side that does not put it back actually becomes larger
y-m-27-06.s.s3.r.d: Compare it with the fact that the original value (2/5) was smaller than 13/25. Write the expression and calculate to check.
y-m-27-06.s.s3.explain: If you put it back, (30/50)²+(20/50)²=13/25=0.52, and if you do not put it back, (30/50)(29/49)+(20/50)(19/49)=25/49≈0.510, so the difference is about 0.01. At the start, it was 13/25=0.52 and 2/5=0.4, a difference of 0.12. The more marbles there are, the less the makeup of the remaining marbles changes even after taking one out, so the difference between the two conditions becomes smaller.

y-m-27-07.title: A fair bet made with two dice
y-m-27-07.topic: Calculating probability: a fair rule decided by the sum of two dice
y-m-27-07.goal: Use the fact that the number of ways to get each sum of the dice differs to judge whether a rule is fair, and make several fair rules yourself and check them.
y-m-27-07.material:
Throw a red die and a blue die at the same time and look at the sum of the numbers. Both dice are fair, and all 36 results (red number, blue number) are considered to occur equally often. The numbers of ways to get each sum are as follows.
Sum 2: 1 way, sum 3: 2 ways, sum 4: 3 ways, sum 5: 4 ways, sum 6: 5 ways, sum 7: 6 ways, sum 8: 5 ways, sum 9: 4 ways, sum 10: 3 ways, sum 11: 2 ways, sum 12: 1 way (36 ways in all when added up)
Yeonu and Seoa want to make "a bet that decides the winner depending on what the sum is". There are no ties, and whatever the sum is, one of the two wins.
y-m-27-07.thinking.0: Judging whether a rule is fair
y-m-27-07.thinking.1: Making several rules that satisfy a condition
y-m-27-07.thinking.2: Explaining why it is fair using the number of cases
y-m-27-07.prereq.0: Experience listing the 36 results of throwing two dice as (red number, blue number)
y-m-27-07.prereq.1: Experience expressing probability as (number of cases) ÷ (total number of cases)
y-m-27-07.s.s1.prompt: The first rule is "If the sum is 6 or less, Yeonu wins, and if it is 7 or more, Seoa wins." Is this rule fair?
y-m-27-07.s.s1.hint.0: In the table with the number of cases for each sum, add up separately the cases for sums of 6 or less and for sums of 7 or more.
y-m-27-07.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the number of kinds of sums and the number of cases are the same.
y-m-27-07.s.s1.o.a: Seoa is more likely to win than Yeonu
y-m-27-07.s.s1.r.a: You compared the cases of sum 6 or less and sum 7 or more by working out the number of cases.
y-m-27-07.s.s1.o.b: It is fair. There are 5 kinds of sums against 6 kinds, which is close
y-m-27-07.s.s1.r.b: It seems you counted only the number of kinds of sums. Check in the table that the number of ways each sum comes up is different.
y-m-27-07.s.s1.o.c: Yeonu has the advantage. Smaller sums come up more often
y-m-27-07.s.s1.r.c: Check in the table whether smaller sums come up more often, using the number of cases for each sum.
y-m-27-07.s.s1.o.d: You can't know until you actually throw
y-m-27-07.s.s1.r.d: The numbers of cases are already fixed, so you can compare the likelihood without throwing.
y-m-27-07.s.s1.explain: The cases with a sum of 6 or less are 1+2+3+4+5=15 ways, and the cases of 7 or more are 6+5+4+3+2+1=21 ways. The probability that Yeonu wins is 15/36 and Seoa's is 21/36, so Seoa has the advantage.
y-m-27-07.s.s2.prompt: Choose 4 different sums that Yeonu wins on (Seoa wins on the remaining sums), and make and enter 3 different fair rules in which the two have exactly the same chance of winning. In each rule the sums are integers from 2 to 12. (Sums a, b, c, d)
y-m-27-07.s.s2.hint.0: Find the number of cases for each sum in the table and look for a combination of 4 that adds up to 18.
y-m-27-07.s.s2.hint.1: Put in the sum with the largest number of cases first, and make the total match with the remaining three sums.
y-m-27-07.s.s2.ok.c1: All four sums are integers from 2 to 12.
y-m-27-07.s.s2.fail.c1: The sums must be integers from 2 to 12.
y-m-27-07.s.s2.ok.c2: The four sums are different from one another.
y-m-27-07.s.s2.fail.c2: The four sums must be different from one another.
y-m-27-07.s.s2.ok.c3: The cases where Yeonu wins are exactly 18 of the 36 ways.
y-m-27-07.s.s2.fail.c3: The total number of cases where Yeonu wins is not 18. Check the number of cases for each sum in the table and add them.
y-m-27-07.s.s2.explain: The number of ways for sum x to come up is 6-|x-7|. If the numbers of cases for the four sums add up to 18, Yeonu and Seoa each have 18 of the 36 ways, so it is fair. Swapping only the order of the same four sums was counted as the same rule.
y-m-27-07.s.s2.because.prompt: Choose one of the rules you made and write why that rule is fair, using the number of cases.
y-m-27-07.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write the number of cases next to each of the four sums you chose and add them.
y-m-27-07.s.s2.because.hint.1: Also write the total number of cases for the remaining sums that Yeonu does not win on.
y-m-27-07.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: The sums Yeonu wins on are ...
y-m-27-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you actually write the four sums of the rule you chose and their numbers of cases?
y-m-27-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you write that 18 of the 36 ways go to Yeonu and the other 18 go to Seoa?
y-m-27-07.s.s2.because.model.0: The numbers of cases for the sums 3, 6, 7, 8 that Yeonu wins on are 2+5+6+5=18 ways. That is half of the 36 ways in all, and Seoa wins on the other 18 ways, so the two have the same chance and it is fair.
y-m-27-07.s.s2.because.model.1: If the sums are 4, 5, 7, 8, it is 3+4+6+5=18 ways, which is half of the 36 ways in all. Seoa also has 18 ways, so the chance of winning is the same and it is fair.
y-m-27-07.s.s3.prompt: Which of the following rules gives Yeonu and Seoa the same chance of winning?
y-m-27-07.s.s3.hint.0: For each rule, find the numbers of cases of the sums Yeonu wins on in the table and add them.
y-m-27-07.s.s3.hint.1: Compare whether the sum is half of 36 (18).
y-m-27-07.s.s3.o.a: Yeonu wins when the sum is a multiple of 5, Seoa wins for any other sum
y-m-27-07.s.s3.r.a: The sums that are multiples of 5 are 5 and 10. Add their numbers of cases from the table and compare with half of 36.
y-m-27-07.s.s3.o.b: Yeonu wins when the sum is 8 or more, Seoa wins when it is 7 or less
y-m-27-07.s.s3.r.b: Add and compare the numbers of cases for the sums of 8 or more and the sums of 7 or less.
y-m-27-07.s.s3.o.c: Yeonu wins when the two numbers are the same, Seoa wins when the two numbers are different
y-m-27-07.s.s3.r.c: Count how many results have the two numbers the same, from (1,1) to (6,6), and compare with 36 ways.
y-m-27-07.s.s3.o.d: Yeonu wins when the sum is even, Seoa wins when the sum is odd
y-m-27-07.s.s3.r.d: You added the numbers of cases of the even sums and the odd sums separately and compared with half of 36.
y-m-27-07.s.s3.explain: The cases where the sum is even are 1+3+5+5+3+1=18 ways and the cases where it is odd are 2+4+6+4+2=18 ways, which are equal. Multiples of 5 (sums 5, 10) are 4+3=7 ways, far short of half of 36; 8 or more is 5+4+3+2+1=15 ways, fewer than 7 or less (21 ways); and the results where the two numbers are the same are 6 ways, far fewer than the 30 where the two numbers are different.

y-m-27-08.title: How much does a best-of-three favor the stronger side?
y-m-27-08.topic: Calculating probability: comparing a best-of-three and a single game when the win rate of one game is the same
y-m-27-08.goal: Predict whether the probability of winning changes with the way of deciding the match (single game, best-of-three) when the win rate of one game is the same, find the missing case in a calculation solution and fix it, and then check whether the prediction holds even when the win rates are equal.
y-m-27-08.material:
Mina and Taeo play a board game. In one game, the probability that Mina wins is 0.6 and the probability that Taeo wins is 0.4, and there are no tied games. The result of each game does not affect the others, and the win rate of one game is considered to be the same for every game.
The two are talking about "Should we decide it with a single game, or a best-of-three (the first to win 2 games wins)?"
y-m-27-08.thinking.1: Finding the case missed in a solution
y-m-27-08.thinking.2: Changing the condition to check your judgment
y-m-27-08.prereq.0: Experience finding the probability of events that do not affect each other happening in succession
y-m-27-08.prereq.1: Experience finding the probability when something can happen in several ways
y-m-27-08.s.s1.prompt: Compared with the probability 0.6 of winning in a single-game match, what do you think Mina's probability of winning the match with a best-of-three will be? Predict it before calculating.
y-m-27-08.s.s1.hint.0: Compare the cases where Taeo wins in a single game with the cases where Taeo wins in a three-game match.
y-m-27-08.s.s1.hint.1: Imagine the cases where Mina wins fewer than 2 games.
y-m-27-08.s.s1.o.a: It gets bigger than 0.6. The more games, the more the skill shows
y-m-27-08.s.s1.r.a: This is the idea that as the number of games increases, the effect of chance decreases. It is a prediction worth checking by calculation.
y-m-27-08.s.s1.o.b: It gets smaller than 0.6. She has to win two games, which is harder
y-m-27-08.s.s1.r.b: You looked only at the number of games she has to win increasing. Also compare the fact that Taeo has to win two games too.
y-m-27-08.s.s1.o.c: It is the same as 0.6. Since the win rate of one game stays the same, it is the same
y-m-27-08.s.s1.r.c: You focused on the win rate of one game being the same. Think about how the effect of a chance single result on the match changes when the number of games increases.
y-m-27-08.s.s1.o.d: It cannot be known from the win rate of one game alone
y-m-27-08.s.s1.r.d: The win rate of one game is given and said to be the same for every game, so you can calculate the probability when the way of deciding the match changes.
y-m-27-08.s.s1.explain: This prediction is a judgment before calculating. Below, check the solution and calculate to see whether the prediction was right.
y-m-27-08.s.s2.prompt: Seoyeon calculated the probability that Mina wins a best-of-three as follows. Choose the one line that is hard to believe. (It can be the line with the wrong process, or the line where the wrong conclusion because of it is written.)
y-m-27-08.s.s2.hint.0: List, in order of wins and losses, all the cases where Mina wins the third game and it becomes 2:1.
y-m-27-08.s.s2.hint.1: Find the probability of each case you listed and count how many were missing from Seoyeon's calculation.
y-m-27-08.s.s2.line.0: In one game, the probability that Mina wins is 0.6 and that she loses is 0.4, and each game does not affect the others.
y-m-27-08.s.s2.line.1: For Mina to win 2:0, she must win both of the first two games, so the probability is 0.6×0.6=0.36.
y-m-27-08.s.s2.line.2: The case where Mina wins 2:1 is only one way (win, lose, win), so the probability is 0.6×0.4×0.6=0.144.
y-m-27-08.s.s2.line.3: Therefore the probability that Mina wins the best-of-three is 0.36+0.144=0.504.
y-m-27-08.s.s2.line.4: 0.504 is smaller than the 0.6 of a single-game match, so a best-of-three is disadvantageous for Mina.
y-m-27-08.s.s2.explain: Lines 1 and 2 are right. Line 3 is the problem. For Mina to win 2:1, there are two ways in which she loses one of the first two games: (win, lose, win) and (lose, win, win). So the probability of 2:1 is 0.6×0.4×0.6×2=0.288. Because of this, the sum in line 4 should be 0.36+0.288=0.648, and the conclusion in line 5 is wrong too.
y-m-27-08.s.s3.prompt: What is the probability that Mina wins a best-of-three?
y-m-27-08.s.s3.hint.0: Divide the ways the match ends into 2:0 and 2:1 and find the probability of each.
y-m-27-08.s.s3.hint.1: Check the number of ways of listing the cases that become 2:1 in order of wins and losses, and the probability they are multiplied by.
y-m-27-08.s.s3.r.a: This is the value that came out of Seoyeon's wrong solution. Check whether you found all the orders that make 2:1.
y-m-27-08.s.s3.r.b: This is the value that adds both the 2:0 case and the two orders that make 2:1.
y-m-27-08.s.s3.r.c: This is the value counting only the cases of winning 2:0. There are also cases where she goes to the third game and wins.
y-m-27-08.s.s3.r.d: This seems like doubling the probability 0.36 of 2:0. The probabilities of the cases that become 2:1 are different values.
y-m-27-08.s.s3.explain: 2:0 is 0.6×0.6=0.36, and 2:1 has two orders, so it is 2×0.6×0.4×0.6=0.288, and the sum is 0.648. The first prediction (it gets bigger than 0.6) was right. If you play all three games and count the cases of winning 2 or more, you get the same value.
y-m-27-08.s.s4.prompt: This time, if the probability that Mina and Taeo win a game is both 0.5, what is the probability that Mina wins a best-of-three?
y-m-27-08.s.s4.hint.0: Compare whether the problem changes if you swap the places of Mina and Taeo.
y-m-27-08.s.s4.hint.1: Calculate the probabilities of 2:0 and 2:1 separately and check what the sum is.
y-m-27-08.s.s4.o.a: It gets bigger than 0.5. The more games, the more advantage Mina has
y-m-27-08.s.s4.r.a: Before, the side with the higher win rate in one game had the advantage. Check whether there is any reason for one side to gain the advantage even when the win rates of the two are the same.
y-m-27-08.s.s4.o.b: It gets smaller than 0.5. She has to win two games, so it is more disadvantageous
y-m-27-08.s.s4.r.b: Taeo has to win two games in just the same way. Compare whether the situations of the two are the same.
y-m-27-08.s.s4.o.c: You can't tell whether it is bigger or smaller than 0.5 without calculating
y-m-27-08.s.s4.r.c: You can check by calculating. However, since the conditions of the two are exactly the same, you can also think of it by symmetry.
y-m-27-08.s.s4.o.d: It is exactly 0.5. Even if the number of games increases, no one gets the advantage
y-m-27-08.s.s4.r.d: You used the fact that it is the same even if the conditions of the two are swapped. If you calculate 0.25+2×0.125, it is 0.5 too.
y-m-27-08.s.s4.explain: If the win rate of one game is the same, 2:0 is 0.5×0.5=0.25, 2:1 is 2×0.5×0.5×0.5=0.25, and the sum is 0.5. The conditions of the two are exactly the same, so the probability of either one winning is the same. Increasing the number of games gives the advantage to 'the side with the higher win rate in one game'; the number of games itself does not favor either side.
